The town of Marrow Bay sits at the end of a single road that winds through pine forest and salt marsh before it reaches the water. For most of the twentieth century the harbour was busy with fishing boats, a small ferry, and the occasional cargo ship carrying timber. The people who lived there knew the tide tables by heart, and the children learned to row before they learned to ride bicycles. The lighthouse on the northern point was tended by a keeper who climbed the spiral stairs twice each night, once at dusk and once before dawn, and who recorded the weather in a ledger that nobody else ever read.

In the nineteen sixties the fishing fleet began to shrink. Nets that had once been mended on the quay were replaced by factory-made lines, and the young men who would have taken over their fathers' boats moved inland to work in the mills. The council commissioned a report on the future of the harbour, and the report recommended a marina for pleasure craft, a cafe on the old pier, and a car park where the ice house had stood. The proposal was debated for three years. Supporters argued that tourism would bring steady income; opponents replied that the sheltered anchorage would soon be filled with yachts that never left their moorings.

By the time the marina opened, the last commercial fishing boat had already been sold. The ice house was demolished, and the cafe served coffee in cups printed with a picture of the lighthouse. Visitors arrived in summer, took photographs of the grey water, and left. The winter population fell below two hundred. The school closed, then reopened as a craft centre. The doctor's surgery became a holiday cottage, and the post office moved into a corner of the pub.

The council hired an engineer from the capital to survey the old pier. His report was thorough. He measured the timbers, tested the mortar, and photographed every crack. He concluded that the pier could be repaired, but that the cost would exceed the budget available by a wide margin. Several of the older fishermen objected to the estimate, saying that the pier had survived worse storms than any the engineer had seen. However, the harbour master refused to sign the survey until the winter gales had passed, and the matter was postponed until spring.

That winter the storms came early. Waves broke over the sea wall and flooded the road as far as the craft centre. The ferry was cancelled for eleven days. In the harbour, two yachts dragged their moorings and were driven onto the rocks below the lighthouse; the lifeboat crew recovered them without injury, though the older boat was badly holed. When the weather cleared, the crew cast off the lines and towed the damaged yachts into the shelter of the inner basin.

In the spring the council met again. The engineer's estimate had not changed, but a grant had become available for coastal heritage projects. The harbour master, who had by then seen the damage for himself, signed the amended survey. Work began in June. Divers reinforced the footings, carpenters replaced the rotting deck, and a new railing was fitted along the seaward edge. Tourists leaned on the railing to watch the water, and the cafe put extra tables outside. The town still loses its young people to the cities, and the winter population is still small, but the pier has lasted another decade, and the lighthouse keeper's ledger sits in a glass case beside the till.
